There are a few mail order companies that specialize in old-style goods with long duty lives. Catalogs like The Vermont Country Store and Buy Me Once. And some books, web sites, vlogs, and podcasts inspired by the old Whole Earth Catalog like Cool Tools and Worldchanging. But one generally needs to learn a little about how things are made and designed to understand what makes them longer-lasting. Going a little further, you can learn to make things for yourself and look for Open Source designs. And you can look to buy things from fine craftsmen rather than big companies, though this usually means spending much more.

One of the interesting things about the lifestyles of the rich is that they spend much less, as a percentage of income, on maintaining their standard of living, high as it is. And this is not just because their incomes are so gigantic but because they can afford to furnish their homes with higher quality goods that don't wear out and either don't depreciate as much or actually appreciate in value. So they're not losing any money when they furnish their homes and, if they take care of their stuff, will actually turn a profit on it when they want to replace it. Imagine if you made money every time you moved. Not possible with our houses full of Walmart crap. Thus many frugal living enthusiasts will suggest that it's better to have fewer things of higher quality.

This tends to exclude high-tech products, however, as there are few alternative means of production for them--something the Open Source movement has long sought to change--and the underlying technology itself goes obsolete rapidly. Computer and communications hardware isn't often designed for planned obsolescence like other consumer products because the underlying technology drives that obsolescence instead. There are certainly higher quality computers, but the notion of a 'luxury' computer is a bit strange. We have seen that with audio gear and cell phones, though.
